column15: One of my favorite projects was during my sophomore year when I worked on a Python task automation script. Typically, finding the parameter for a task involves a version of educated guess and check, which is incredibly slow (especially when using the computing cluster). This project was my first introduction to Python automation and I really enjoyed working on the project since this same automation code would be used for my (and many others’) current research work. There were several challenges in this project. The most notable challenge was the issue of our processes being preempted from the computing cluster, which essentially throws away any parameter searching that was done up til then. The fix was to add a separate checking mechanism, which would automatically resubmit the script if the job ever got kicked off the computer.

This summer, I built Compiled (https://jackstuehler.com/compiled), a website for comparing colleges based on academic and career outcomes for specific majors. I was frustrated by how difficult it was to compare this information across schools, so I used data from the Department of Education’s College Scorecard to build a tool that lets users compare schools in a table or visualize them on an interactive scatterplot.

I built Compiled using Next.js, TypeScript, and MySQL, using AI tools throughout development to help me learn unfamiliar technologies while applying what I already knew. One of the biggest challenges was working with the College Scorecard data itself. The raw datasets were large and messy, so I had to figure out how to filter and restructure them into a database containing the information I actually needed. I also spent a lot of time thinking about which features would be most useful to a user. One of the features I’m most proud of is the interactive scatterplot, which has configurable axes and drag-to-zoom. 

I also spent time optimizing the site after deployment, eventually achieving Lighthouse performance scores of 98/100 on mobile and 100/100 on desktop. This was important to me because I had been frustrated by how slow other college data websites could be when trying to compare schools.

The project I am most proud of is a Tetris-playing agent. The architecture behind the project is a transformer, tokenizing each row and column individually, with an extra column token for meta information (score, next piece, etc). The model is trained using PPO, and I did something I think is interesting for the reward shaping. Obviously we give the model a reward for scoring, and a punishment for topping out/trying to make illegal moves (the logits are defined on a placement level rather than a frame level, as training each individual input is impractical. This does however create the problem that the model tries to output impossible logits sometimes, eg trying to place a piece that is blocked by a previous piece. So we just give the model a flat cost for trying to place the pieces somewhere it cant). But one specific direction I explored was the aggression of the model. 

Previous models had arbitrary aggression settings, which just amounted to scaling the reward for points and reducing the reward for topout, but I wanted to make this relationship explicit. I wanted a model that could be fine-tuned to topout a specific percentage of the time before level 29 (the "killscreen"). To do this, I used a Lagrange multiplier. If we attach a cost head to the transformer base, then we can have the model make predictions about the %cost, essentially risk, of each placement causing the model to top out. We can then constrain the model to limit the sum of these cost evaluations to below whatever we want (we can do this because the episodes are capped at level 29, so the sums are finite) and voila, we have a model that plays as aggressively as possible while topping out c% of the time. Topping out means losing if that wasn't clear before. 

The development of this project was super challenging but fun, and I learned a ton about reinforcement learning along the way. I would say the main challenge was trying to distill current best Tetris agents into my model. The bulk of the time spent training a model to play Tetris is spent at the beginning, where the model is just trying to figure out how to place the pieces and score. Because we only reward for scoring, the rewards are extremely sparse at the beginning of training, making this stage of training very tedious. 

To combat this, I tried several methods of distillation, and the failure of each of these methods taught me a LOT about RL as a whole, especially policy distributions. Usually what would happen is I would get a model that agreed with the top engines around 95-99% of the time, which I thought was great and then would start RL finetuning. The problem was, the model would quickly diverge from the distribution of states it was trained on, these states being the rollouts from the teacher model, and would have no idea what to do in these unfamiliar states and would top out at extremely low scores. This is fine on its own, but the problem was then the model had to learn how to deal with these situations, and then its distilled policy would get overwritten, essentially starting from scratch. Eventually I consulted the RL literature and found a technique called DAgger, where the teacher and student alternate placements during rollouts, with the teacher making less and less of the moves as the stages of DAgger increased. This resulted in a much better distillation process and faster training overall.

For that reason, an LRU cache for O(1) lookup with a hash map worked the best. Within Ignition, the program relied mostly on Jython and SQL. I kind of went into detail on my VulcanForms data project in the first section, but here I might as well talk about my sushi go bot. I've also built several websites (with plenty of vibe coding involved), but these are obviously less, like, algorithmic. 

It was right after the sushi go project from CS11, and I was bored in my dorm before the end of finals period, so I thought I should try to play sushi go optimally. I basically just added a bot player that uses some basic information set monte carlo tree search to play sushi go, decently. It runs simulations for every turn. The bot keeps track of which cards have appeared in the round, so it can have more realistic simulations. Each node of the tree is basically the next card picked in the sequence (selects randomly based on untried cards in current hand). As each node is built, a simulated game (using a simple greedy algorithm) plays out from that card pick, the final score is calculated for that node, and its visit count increases by 1. When choosing which node to explore next, the bot balances exploration and exploitation using the UCB1 algorithm, and continues as normal. The bot plays 15000 simulations per turn, adding new nodes with randomly selected untried cards when possible, or just reevaluating the score of each path with greedy simulations (and randomized cards in play when it hasn't seen them all yet). One project I am especially proud of is a cost-optimized LLM query router. I built it to reduce the cost of using paid language models by classifying each prompt based on its complexity and routing simpler requests to a free, locally hosted model while reserving GPT-4o for more difficult requests. I also added context compression before paid API calls to reduce token usage. The system reduced total inference costs by over 70% while retaining about 92% of the baseline accuracy.

The main challenge was finding the right balance between cost and response quality. An overly aggressive router saved more money but sometimes sent difficult prompts to the smaller model, while a conservative router reduced the potential savings. I tested different classification approaches and thresholds, analyzed where routing errors occurred, and adjusted the system based on those results. This project excited me because it combined machine learning, software engineering, and practical product tradeoffs.

column15:
The project that I’m most proud of is a personal project that I started during my first comp sci class and have been working on ever sense. We were working in Java, and we had just learned how to render things on the screen. I was interested in learning about how computers render things in 3 dimensions, not just the 2 dimensions that we were doing in class. 

I embarked on a project to make my own 3d renderer completely from scratch (no libraries outside the ones baked into java, and once AI released I vowed not to use AI to write code for this specific project because it was meant as a self exploration project.) I did research on all the math and physics needed for the project, and worked on it on and off for the next 2 years. 

I got it to the point where I could upload and render custom 3d obj files with textures, colors, and lighting (so you were able to upload 3d models from a CAD software or a 3d modeling software like Blendr and render them and move around and explore the models). I started with perspective projection, but also experimented with orthographic projection, as well as basic lighting, ray tracing, UV mapping for textures, and many optimization techniques for getting things to render at a reasonable framerate (30-60fps) on a cpu (didn’t have a gpu or anything to render things on). 

It may not sound incredibly impressive, but I am extremely proud of it because it was an entirely self taught journey that allowed me to explore my love for math, physics, and coding. It showed me that I am capable of a lot more than I initially thought if I just apply myself.

The two biggest challenges I faced were layering and optimization:

The first problem that occured was layering. I tried for several months to figure out a way to sort the triangles in an order such that when they were rendered, they didn’t overlap with each other or render behind one another. I tried every method I could, but all of them seemed to have some sort of edge case that would break the rendering. The one method that I was avoiding, even though it was the one that was considered the best method to use, was pixel-by-pixel rendering. I was avoiding this, because I knew it meant I would have to step up my optimization game significantly. 
This moves us to the second problem, optimization. Once I switched to pixel-by-pixel rendering, my layering issues were entirely resolved, but the framerate had significantly dropped. I needed to find a way to determine which triangle should be rendered for every single pixel (>1 million pixels), which was an extremely expensive task, especially considering it couldn’t really be paralleled onto a gpu because I was programming just for a cpu. From here, I spent the next several months working to improve every tiny piece of my code to make it run as fast as possible, and eventually I got it back up to the desired 30-60fps.

The project I'm proudest of came out of my internship this past summer at Dassault Systèmes, working across QE, R&D, and data science. The problem I was handed was that nobody could answer a simple question: what parts of the product aren't being tested? The coverage data existed, but it was scattered across separate systems in formats that didn't talk to each other, so leadership was making decisions about where to put testing effort largely on instinct.
I built a tool that consolidated those fragmented sources into one place and rendered the result as an interactive network diagram, components as nodes, their relationships as edges, coverage gaps visible as soon as you looked at it. The technical work was the data layer: reconciling sources that named the same component three different ways, deciding what counted as a gap, and getting it to a state where the numbers were trustworthy enough for someone to act on.
The harder challenge wasn't the code. It was that the answer depended on people in four different functions who each had a piece of the picture and each defined "coverage" slightly differently. I spent a lot of the internship in conversations — with QE engineers, R&D, data science, and PMs — working out what they actually needed to see rather than what I assumed they did. The visualization went through several versions because the first one answered my question and not theirs. That taught me that the useful part of a tool is almost never the part that was hard to build.
Right now I'm building something in that same spirit: "Jumbo Wasn't From Here Either," a resource tool for international students navigating early careers Students build a profile — year in school, country of origin (travel restrictions matter more than people realize), the industry they want to explore — and the tool surfaces what's actually available to them, including a tab for Tufts students looking for on-campus work. I'm keeping it free while I build credibility with it. The challenge here is the same one I ran into at Dassault from the other direction: the information mostly exists, it's just scattered and hard to act on, and the real work is talking to the people who need it before deciding what to build.

African Bridge Network is my first choice without hesitation. I'm on the pre-law track, planning to practice immigration and employee rights law, and this project sits exactly at that intersection: skilled immigrants who already have the qualifications, losing time and opportunity to certification processes nobody has mapped for them. I've spent a lot of my life and my work around people navigating systems that weren't designed with them in mind, and I'd bring that context to the requirements conversations, not just the code. Building the tool that makes a mentee's progress and outstanding requirements visible in one place is a version of the work I want to do for a career.
Mystic Learning Center and Just A Start are my next two because both are essentially social work problems with a technical layer on top, and access for people who are disadvantaged is what draws me to this kind of work in the first place. Mystic's paper-based enrollment asks low-income families to fill out the same information repeatedly to reach subsidized childcare they're already entitled to, the barrier isn't eligibility, it's paperwork, which is the most fixable kind of barrier there is. Just A Start is the same problem seen from the staff side: a decade of trusted community relationships scattered across inboxes and personal contacts, so a client's referral depends on which staff member happens to be in the room. Making that knowledge searchable means help reaches people more consistently, and consistency is usually what's missing.
Teen Empowerment is fourth, and it's the project where my technical background lines up most directly. Last summer I built a tool that consolidated fragmented test data from several systems into a single interactive visualization so leadership could actually see where the gaps were, the same shape of problem as pulling IMPOWR data into dashboards and North Star metrics. I'd also be curious about the AI-assisted theme coding, particularly the part where staff stay in control of interpreting the output. That framing matters to me: the tool should sharpen what people already know about their own programs, not replace their reading of it. Youth organizing is a little further from my own background than the three above it, which is the only reason it isn't higher. 
The bottom four are all causes I care about, and I'd be happy to spend the year building for any of them, the order just reflects where I think I'd contribute most.

A project that I really enjoyed working on was Trackstar. Trackstar is a Python-based DJ controller that uses webcam hand-tracking to control and mix songs in real time through an integrated DJ interface. This was a really exciting project to work on since it was the first project I worked on together with a friend, and we had a lot of friends who knew how to DJ and could actually use our program.

We built the program in Python and connected the hand-tracking output to functions that controlled different parts of the DJ software. One technical challenge we faced was managing the state of our hand-tracking inputs. Because the webcam processed frames continuously, a single hand gesture could trigger the same function multiple times before the gesture changed. This caused commands to execute repeatedly when they were only supposed to execute once. We solved this by implementing state checks that compared the current detected gesture with the previous frame before executing a command.

My first ever hand-coded project was the final project for CS10: an "evil hangman" where the program never picks a word but instead holds a list of words and reacts depending on user input. Whenever the user makes a guess, it secretly looks for a different word within the list and outputs an error message. It only accepts a letter when it's out of options.

The most exciting part of the whole project was realizing that the program doesn't need an answer to proceed. However, this was also the hardest part: making the lie undetectable. I remember my first version just grabbed any word without the user's letter, which broke immediately. The board would show "-I---", then the program would swap to a word like "KIWI" where the board would update to "-I-I", and suddenly that would be incorrect. It took a lot of back and forth to come up with a way to ensure that the player couldn't prove I was lying.

It was not a super significant program, but it was a great opportunity to put what I learned throughout the semester into a mini project, and to think from the user's perspective rather than just about what my code did.

column15: A project I am really proud of is my Sushi Go final project from CS 11.  The goal of this project was to create a game of Sushi Go that involved 2 players and a deck of cards. I implemented the program so that each player took turns choosing a card from the full deck and added it to their personal deck, and the one with the most points won. This project was interesting to me because there were so many moving parts at once. I had to keep track of the deck, each player's personal deck, as well as the deck they had to transfer over to the other person. The project was challenging at first because it was hard to conceptualize what needed to happen each round. However, the main thing that helped me was drawing out each of the steps and outlining the processes I wanted each function to perform. The project also involved a lot of file reading and making sure the program could run with different types of decks. It was also important for me to keep track of the order of operations because it wouldn’t make sense for me to declare a winner before both players went, or to reveal the cards before one was picked from the deck. The project truly allowed me to see problems from a close view as well as a broader perspective. I think these skills will be helpful when developing websites that will be used from hundreds of people because I’ll be able to focus on testing a variety of scenarios.

I think it would be developing a networking agent during my internship at a healthcare venture studio this summer. One challenge that the company faced was that every new venture had to find potential design partners from scratch and this process could take weeks. I built an agent designed to automate this to build their efficiency and create a network of healthcare provider groups that the studio would engage and then could eventually draw on across different ventures

I designed an end-to-end workflow in n8n rather than just building a single AI tool. The agent continuously identifies provider groups that fit specific criteria, finds relevant decision makers, and uses Claude to evaluate and prioritise the strongest prospects. It then moves those prospects into an outreach campaign (Instantly), tracks replies, and uses that feedback to refine which types of groups it prioritises in future searches.

One of the biggest challenges was in the design itself, to decide what should actually be automated. We wanted the agent to handle the repetitive work of finding, evaluating and tracking potential partners but without trying to automate the relationship itself. Also, the workflow had to connect several different platforms via APIs/MCP, so thinking through what information needed to move between each tool and how the different steps would fit together reliably and eventually building those connections was the most challenging step.

column15: When I as in high school I was inspired by an online art generator to make an ASCII art converter that looped through pixels and based on their intensity assigned a character to each one (or group of pixels depending on image size), resulting in a character version of the artwork. This project had many parts and was larger than I was used to at the time, so I couldn't just write the whole thing and then debug as I usually did. This taught me to test incrementally and code with modularity.
